questions.stem: What are gametes?
questions.why: Gametes are the sex cells: sperm in males, oocytes or eggs in females.

options.why: Somatic cells are every cell except the sex cells.
A zygote is the product of fertilization, not a gamete.
Gametes are haploid, not diploid.

questions.stem: Why are gametes described as haploid?
questions.why: Haploid means a single set: 23 individual chromosomes. At fertilization the two sets unite into 23 pairs, or 46 total.

options.why: 46 is the diploid count found in body cells.
Gametes carry autosomes as well as one sex chromosome.
23 pairs is 46 chromosomes, which is diploid — the zygote, not the gamete.

questions.stem: What is a zygote?
questions.why: A zygote is the first fertilized cell. It is diploid, carrying two of each of the 23 chromosomes — one set from each parent.

options.why: The zygote is diploid, which is what fertilization produced.
Implantation happens well after the zygote stage.
An unfertilized egg is an oocyte and is still haploid.

questions.stem: How many of the 23 chromosome pairs are autosomes?
questions.why: 22 pairs are autosomes, meaning not sex chromosomes. The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes.

options.t: 22 — the rest is the sex pair

options.why: Only one pair determines sex, not two.
The 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes, so not all are autosomes.
Only one pair determines sex, not three.

questions.stem: Which sex chromosome combination produces a male?
questions.why: Both males and females carry an X. If the partner chromosome is a second X a female develops; if it is a Y, a male develops.

options.why: Everyone carries at least one X; YY does not occur.

options.t: One X only, with no partner
options.why: A single unpaired X is not the normal male pattern.
Two X chromosomes produce a female.

questions.stem: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?
questions.why: Genotype is the arrangement of genes and their characteristics. Phenotype is the characteristic that results when those genes are expressed.

options.t: Genotype is the gene arrangement; phenotype is what is expressed
Genotype is inherited; phenotype is acquired after birth
options.why: Phenotype is the expression of inherited genes, not something acquired.

options.t: Genotype covers autosomes; phenotype covers sex chromosomes
options.why: Both terms apply to all chromosomes, not one group each.

options.t: Genotype is what is expressed; phenotype is the gene arrangement
options.why: This reverses the two terms.

questions.stem: Which are the essential organs of the male reproductive system?
questions.why: The testes are the essential organs, forming both sperm cells and male sex hormones. Everything else is accessory or supporting.

options.why: Those are accessory glands, which supply fluid rather than gametes.
Those are supporting structures, not the essential organs.
Those are ducts that store and transport sperm, not produce it.

questions.stem: How does the scrotum respond to cold temperature?
questions.why: Cold makes the scrotum contract and wrinkle, moving the testes closer to the pelvic cavity. Warmth relaxes it so the testes sit about 3°C below body temperature, which sperm need.

options.t: It has no response to temperature
options.why: The cremaster and dartos muscles react specifically to temperature.

options.t: It relaxes, letting the testes hang lower
options.why: Relaxing and hanging loosely is the response to warmth, not cold.

options.t: It contracts, drawing the testes upward
It thickens to insulate the testes
options.why: The cremaster and dartos muscles move the testes rather than thicken.

questions.stem: Which structure within the testis produces sperm cells?
questions.why: Sperm are produced in the spermatogenic (seminiferous) tubules. The interstitial cells between them secrete testosterone.

options.why: Interstitial cells sit between the tubules and secrete testosterone.
Efferent ductules carry sperm onward to the epididymis.
The rete testis is a passage sperm travel through after production.

questions.stem: Which cells secrete testosterone?
questions.why: Interstitial cells lie between the seminiferous tubules and secrete testosterone.

options.why: The epididymis stores and matures sperm.
The seminiferous tubules make sperm, not hormones.
The prostate secretes seminal fluid, not testosterone.

questions.stem: Why do the testes belong to two body systems?
questions.why: Producing testosterone makes the testes endocrine organs; producing sperm makes them reproductive organs.

options.t: They filter blood and make sperm
options.why: The testes do not filter blood.
Semen is supplied by the accessory glands, not the testes.

options.t: They make sperm and store it
options.why: Storage happens in the epididymis, and both listed roles are reproductive.

questions.stem: Which is a male secondary sex characteristic driven by testosterone?
questions.why: Testosterone enlarges the larynx and thickens the vocal folds, lowering voice pitch. It also increases body hair, thickens skin, builds muscle and bone, and reduces scalp hair.

options.why: Testosterone decreases scalp hair growth rather than increasing it.
Pelvic widening is a female secondary characteristic.
Mammary duct growth is driven by female sex hormones.

questions.stem: Besides sex characteristics, what else does testosterone increase?
questions.why: Testosterone increases cellular metabolism and the production of red blood cells.

options.why: Immune cell production is not a testosterone effect.
Plasma proteins and bile are liver functions.
Insulin and glucose handling are pancreatic functions.

questions.stem: What is the male climacteric?
questions.why: The male climacteric is the period marking a decrease in testosterone level and a decline in sexual function.

options.t: The point sperm become independently motile
options.why: Motility is a stage of sperm maturation, unrelated to the climacteric.
The climacteric marks decline, not peak.

options.t: The onset of sperm production at puberty
options.why: That describes puberty, at the start of reproductive life.

questions.stem: Which structure do sperm reach immediately after the seminiferous tubules?
questions.why: The path runs seminiferous tubules, rete testis, efferent ductules, epididymis, ductus deferens, ejaculatory duct, urethra.

options.why: The ductus deferens comes after the epididymis.
The epididymis comes after the efferent ductules, not immediately.
The ejaculatory duct is second to last, just before the urethra.

questions.stem: What is the function of the epididymis?
questions.why: The epididymis is a tightly coiled tube connected to the testis that stores and protects spermatozoa and aids their maturation.

options.why: Production happens in the seminiferous tubules.

options.t: Secreting most of the semen volume
options.why: Most semen volume comes from the seminal vesicles.
The urethra delivers semen out of the body.

questions.stem: How long do sperm remain viable stored in the tail of the epididymis?
questions.why: Sperm remain viable in the tail of the epididymis for 40 to 60 days. Transit from head to tail takes about 20 days.

options.why: That is far shorter than the actual storage window.
20 days is the transit time through the epididymis, not the viability window.
120 days is the lifespan of a red blood cell.

questions.stem: What happens to sperm that are not ejaculated?
questions.why: Unejaculated sperm disintegrate and are picked up by the epididymal blood vessels for reabsorption.

options.why: Storage is limited to roughly 40 to 60 days.

options.t: They pass out in the urine
options.why: Sperm are not excreted through the urinary route.

options.t: They return to the seminiferous tubules
options.why: Movement through the duct system runs one way only.

questions.stem: What do the seminal vesicles contribute to semen?
questions.why: Seminal vesicles supply nearly 60% of semen volume as a slightly alkaline fluid containing fructose, which fuels the sperm.

options.t: The sperm cells, about 10% of volume
options.why: Sperm come from the testes, not an accessory gland.
Lubricating mucus comes from the bulbourethral glands.
That describes the prostate's contribution.

questions.stem: What is the main effect of prostatic fluid?
questions.why: The prostate secretes a thin, white, alkaline fluid that neutralizes the acidic fluid carrying sperm, enhances motility, and helps neutralize vaginal acidity.

options.why: The prostate does not coat individual sperm.

options.t: Lubricating the end of the penis
options.why: Lubrication is the bulbourethral glands' role.

options.t: Supplying fructose as an energy source
options.why: Fructose comes from the seminal vesicles.

questions.stem: When do the bulbourethral glands secrete?
questions.why: Bulbourethral (Cowper) glands secrete a mucus-like alkaline fluid in response to sexual stimulation, lubricating the end of the penis.

options.t: Only at the moment of ejaculation
options.why: They secrete before ejaculation, to lubricate.
Their secretion is triggered rather than constant.
Their function is reproductive, not urinary.

questions.stem: What proportion of semen volume is actually sperm?
questions.why: Semen is roughly 60% seminal vesicle fluid, 30% prostatic fluid, and only 10% sperm.

options.why: 60% is the seminal vesicle share.
Sperm are a small fraction of the total volume.
30% is the prostatic fluid share.

questions.stem: How many sperm does semen contain per millilitre?
questions.why: Semen contains between 20 and 150 million sperm per mL, with 2 to 5 mL released at one time.

options.why: That is well below the normal range.
The count is in the millions, not thousands.
That overstates the normal concentration.

questions.stem: What triggers an erection at the vessel level?
questions.why: Parasympathetic fibers trigger nitric oxide release, relaxing smooth muscle in penile vessels and dilating the arterioles so blood floods in.

options.t: Nitric oxide relaxing vascular smooth muscle

options.why: The trigger is parasympathetic and dilatory, not sympathetic constriction.
Testosterone governs sex characteristics, not the acute vascular response.
Erection is vascular, not driven by skeletal muscle compression.

questions.stem: What distinguishes emission from ejaculation?
questions.why: Emission is movement of sperm and gland secretions into the urethra. Ejaculation is release of that semen through the urethra to outside the body.

options.t: Emission precedes arousal; ejaculation follows it
options.why: Both events follow arousal, not precede it.

options.t: Emission empties the urethra; ejaculation fills it
options.why: This reverses the two terms.

options.t: Emission is the sensation; ejaculation is the muscular event
options.why: Both are physical events in sequence — emission moves fluid into the urethra, ejaculation expels it.

options.t: Emission fills the urethra; ejaculation empties it

questions.stem: Which organ is NOT part of the female reproductive system?
questions.why: The principal organs are the ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina, mammary glands, and external genitalia. The bladder belongs to the urinary system.

options.why: Fallopian tubes are internal accessory organs.
Mammary glands are listed among the principal organs.
The cervix is the inferior portion of the uterus.

questions.stem: Which substance secreted by the ovaries controls pituitary FSH?
questions.why: The ovaries secrete inhibin, which is involved in the feedback control of pituitary FSH production.

options.why: Estrogen drives female characteristics and the cycle, not FSH feedback specifically.
Progesterone regulates the cycle and supports pregnancy.
Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary, not the ovary.

questions.stem: About 20 follicles begin maturing each cycle. How many release an ovum?
questions.why: About 20 follicles begin maturation each month, but only a single follicle matures fully and releases an ovum. The rest degenerate and are reabsorbed.

options.why: Only a single follicle completes maturation.
The rest die off and are reabsorbed.
Ovulation occurs in every cycle after menarche.

questions.stem: When does meiosis in primary oocytes resume?
questions.why: Primary oocytes begin meiosis early in fetal development, stop, and do not restart until puberty.

options.why: Meiosis begins in fetal life but then halts.
Fertilization is much later than the resumption point.
Menopause marks the end of the reproductive years.

questions.stem: Where does fertilization usually occur?
questions.why: Fertilization usually occurs in the fallopian tubes as the oocyte travels toward the uterus.

options.why: The oocyte must be released before it can be fertilized.
The uterus is where implantation occurs, after fertilization.
The cervix is a passage, not a fertilization site.

questions.stem: What moves the oocyte along the fallopian tube?
questions.why: The tube is lined with secretory cells and cilia, and oocyte transport combines ciliary movement with smooth muscle contractions.

options.why: Transport is active rather than positional.

options.t: Cilia alone, with no muscular help
options.why: Smooth muscle contraction contributes alongside the cilia.
Follicular fluid does not propel the oocyte down the tube.

questions.stem: How long after ovulation can fertilization occur?
questions.why: Fertilization can occur at any time within about a 24-hour window after ovulation.

options.why: Seven days is far beyond the viable window.
The window is longer than that.
The window is shorter than that.

questions.stem: Which uterine layer is shed and rebuilt each cycle?
questions.why: The endometrium is the inner mucosal layer that changes with the phases of the uterine cycle and receives the implanting embryo.

options.why: The perimetrium is the outer serosal covering.
The cervical canal is a passage, not a layer.
The myometrium is muscle and is not shed.

questions.stem: Which uterine layer contracts to expel the fetus during childbirth?
questions.why: The myometrium is composed of three layers of muscle fibers whose contractions help expel the fetus during childbirth.

options.why: The endometrium is mucosal lining, not muscle.
The peritoneum lines the abdominal cavity generally.
The perimetrium is the outer serosal covering.

questions.stem: Why is the vaginal environment acidic?
questions.why: The vagina is acidic to inhibit bacterial growth. Alkaline prostatic and bulbourethral secretions counteract that acidity for the sperm.

options.why: Contractions are hormonally driven, not pH driven.
Mucus consistency is controlled by cycle hormones.
Acidity actually hinders sperm, which is why prostatic fluid is alkaline.

questions.stem: Which glands provide lubrication during intercourse?
questions.why: Bartholin glands produce mucus for lubrication during intercourse.

options.why: Bulbourethral glands are male accessory glands.
Sebaceous glands are skin oil glands.
Mammary glands produce milk.

questions.stem: What type of gland is a mammary gland?
questions.why: The mammary glands are modified sweat glands housed within the breasts, and their main purpose is lactation.

options.why: Mammary glands secrete outward through ducts rather than into blood.
Sebaceous glands produce oil, not milk.
Lymph nodes near the breast are separate structures.

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates milk production?
questions.why: Prolactin, an anterior pituitary hormone, stimulates milk production. Oxytocin, from the posterior pituitary, stimulates its ejection.

options.why: Estrogen drives breast development, not milk synthesis.
Oxytocin ejects milk that has already been produced.
Progesterone supports pregnancy rather than lactation.

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates ejection of milk into the ducts?
questions.why: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary stimulates ejection of milk into the ducts of the mammary glands.

options.why: LH triggers ovulation.
Prolactin produces the milk rather than ejecting it.
Inhibin regulates pituitary FSH.

questions.stem: The female external accessory organs together compose what?
questions.why: The external accessory organs surround the openings of the urethra and vagina, composing the vulva (pudendum).

options.why: The hymen is a single membrane at the vaginal orifice.
The vestibule is the cleft between the labia majora.
The perineum is the muscular floor region, not the organ group.

questions.stem: What is the clitoris composed of?
questions.why: The clitoris consists of erectile tissue and nerves. The labia minora converge anteriorly to form its hoodlike covering.

options.why: It is not a secretory structure.
Cartilage is not present in the clitoris.
That describes the hymen.

questions.stem: What is the typical range for menstrual cycle duration?
questions.why: Cycle duration differs from woman to woman, ranging from 24 to 35 days.

options.why: 28 days is the average used for diagrams, not a fixed value.
That is longer than the normal range.
That is shorter than the normal range.

questions.stem: At what age does menarche typically occur?
questions.why: Menarche is the onset of first menses, occurring when a girl reaches childbearing age between 11 and 14 years.

options.why: That range is menopause, not menarche.
That is earlier than the typical range.
That is later than the typical range.

questions.stem: At what age does menopause typically occur?
questions.why: Menopause, the female climacteric, is the last menses, typically between 40 and 50 years.

options.why: That is earlier than the typical range.
That range is menarche, the first menses.
That is later than the typical range.

questions.stem: Which days make up the follicular phase?
questions.why: The ovarian cycle divides into the follicular phase, days 1 to 13, and the luteal phase, days 14 to 28.

options.why: That is the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle.
That is the luteal phase.
That is the secretory phase of the uterine cycle.

questions.stem: Which hormone peaks trigger the follicle to rupture?
questions.why: FSH develops the follicles and LH stimulates hormone secretion. Peak levels of estrogen and LH then cause the mature follicle to rupture.

options.why: Neither of these triggers ovulation.
FSH develops the follicle earlier; progesterone dominates afterward.
Prolactin governs lactation, not ovulation.

questions.stem: What happens to the corpus luteum if fertilization does NOT occur?
questions.why: Without fertilization the corpus luteum shrinks, stops secreting hormones, and is gradually absorbed into the ovarian tissue.

options.why: The placenta forms from embryonic and uterine tissue.

options.t: It is shed with the endometrium
options.why: It remains in the ovary rather than being shed.
Continued secretion happens only when fertilization occurs.

questions.stem: What happens during the proliferative phase?
questions.why: The proliferative phase, days 5 to 14, is after menstruation and before ovulation. The endometrium thickens to prepare to receive a fertilized oocyte.

options.why: Follicle rupture is an ovarian event at day 14.
Corpus luteum regression is a late luteal event.
Shedding is menstruation, at the start of the cycle.

questions.stem: Which days make up the secretory phase?
questions.why: The secretory phase runs days 15 to 28, from ovulation until menstruation, with the lining continuing to thicken.

options.why: That is the proliferative phase.
That is roughly the menstrual period itself.
That is the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle.

questions.stem: Match each male reproductive structure to its function.
questions.why: Two structures inside the testis do production; the epididymis does storage; three accessory glands supply the fluid. Note that sperm are only about 10% of semen volume.
pairs: Stores and protects sperm, aiding maturation
Secrete fructose-rich fluid — about 60% of semen volume
Secretes alkaline fluid enhancing sperm motility
Secrete mucus-like fluid lubricating the end of the penis

questions.stem: Match each female reproductive structure to its function.
questions.why: Ovary produces, tube transports, endometrium receives, myometrium delivers. The uterine wall layers are the set most worth memorizing cold.
pairs: Produce oocytes and secrete estrogen, progestins, and inhibin
Connect ovaries to uterus; usual site of fertilization
Inner uterine layer where the embryo implants
Muscular layer whose contractions expel the fetus
Narrowest part of the uterus, opening into the vagina

questions.stem: Match each phase of the menstrual cycle to its days and events.
questions.why: Two parallel cycles running at once. The ovarian phases split at ovulation on day 14; the uterine phases split at the same point, which is why the two stay synchronized.
pairs: Days 1 to 13 — follicle develops and ruptures at ovulation
Days 14 to 28 — corpus luteum secretes hormones or regresses
Days 5 to 14 — endometrium thickens to receive an oocyte
Days 15 to 28 — lining thickens further, then sheds if no fertilization
